title: Contrastive Identification and Generation in the Limit
claim: Unlike positive-example streams, unordered pairs crossing a hidden boundary still constrain labels up to one flip per connected component.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, hidden dashed cut in middle, grouped components in right panel
description: Three side-by-side panels sharing one target. Panel (a), titled 'text', shows five blue filled dots labeled x1 to x5 on the left, with gray hollow dots (negatives) on the right. The caption below reads 'one positive per round'. Panel (b), 'contrastive presentation', shows four black line segments joining hollow circles, each crossing a vertical dashed gray curve labeled 'hidden cut'. The caption reads 'one unordered pair per round'. No point is marked positive. Panel (c), 'what the learner can infer', repeats the pairs from (b), grouped into light gray rounded blobs by connected component. Each blob has a '±' tag showing a hidden global flip. The caption reads 'labels up to one flip per component'. The eye goes first to the blue dots at left, then to the dashed cut.
caption: Three views of one target ℎ; positives are on the left. (a) A text shows positives. (b) A contrastive presentation shows pairs that cross the unknown cut between supp(ℎ) and its complement, and it never marks a point. (c) Every observed pair crosses the cut, so on each connected component of the observed graph the labels are fixed up to one hidden flip (Remark 4.10).
abstract: In identification in the limit (Gold, 1967), a learner reads positive examples and must eventually name the target hypothesis; in generation in the limit (Kleinberg and Mullainathan, 2024), it must eventually produce new positive examples. We study a weaker, relational signal: each observation is an unordered pair $\{x,y\}$ with $h(x)\neq h(y)$, such as a cannot-link constraint or a dissimilar-pair label, and the learner never learns which point is positive. All our results come from one object: a pair is valid for every member of a finite family exactly when its points lie in antipodal cells of the family's membership map. (1) For every corruption budget $k$, known or unknown, we characterize exactly the identifiable classes. Incomparable hypotheses must cover the domain and share more than $2k$ points, and Angluin's tell-tale sets must survive the loss of $2k$ points. Every unbounded budget makes any two hypotheses confusable. (2) A contrastive closure dimension characterizes uniform generation. On finite classes, generation fails exactly when a family that shares a presentation has a finite common support; on countable classes this finite condition no longer suffices. (3) On clean data the four learning criteria form a strict diamond. (4) Under corruption the order changes: some classes are identifiable from contrastive pairs under every finite budget by one algorithm, but not from positive examples with one corrupted example.
